title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (1 of 7)
hook: the most famous book about yoga opens with one word, and the word is now
tomorrow: Patanjali 1.2: the stilling of the mind's turnings (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dvaita and beyond closed: I want to taste sugar, not become sugar. Two, and the space between is love. Today a new week, and a new book. Day two hundred ninety-five.
screen: `TWO, AND THE SPACE BETWEEN IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Think about how you start things. The gym, in January. The diet, on Monday. The meditation app, once work calms down. There's always a better time coming, and it's never quite this one. Now picture the most famous book ever written about yoga. Not the poses: the mind. It's about two thousand years old, give or take a few centuries, and it has shaped nearly every serious yoga teacher since. You might expect it to open with a warning, or a promise, or a long list of what you need first. It opens with one word. And the word is now.
screen: `MONDAY. JANUARY. WHEN THINGS CALM DOWN.` → `THE BOOK OF YOGA.` → `ITS FIRST WORD: NOW.`

segments.voice: The book is the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. A sutra is a thread: a short line, packed tight, meant to be memorized and then unpacked by a teacher. There are about a hundred and ninety-five of them, in four chapters. Who was Patanjali? Honestly, we don't know much. Scholars' guesses for the text span centuries, from about twenty-two hundred years ago to about fifteen hundred. Tradition tells beautiful stories about him, including that he was an incarnation of the great serpent who holds up the world. The first thread, in Sanskrit, is atha yoga anushasanam. Now, the teaching of yoga. Atha, now. It's a word Sanskrit books often start with. The Brahma Sutras open the same way: now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman. Traditionally the word is also considered auspicious, a good sound to begin with. The oldest commentary on the Yoga Sutras says atha marks a beginning: here the teaching starts. But teachers have always found more in it. Now means the preparation is over. Now means you've arrived with whatever brought you here, a restless mind, a bad week, curiosity. Now means yoga isn't something that happens after your life gets sorted out. It's the sorting. This week we'll walk the first sixteen threads, slowly. Tomorrow, the famous definition of what yoga actually is. Today, just the first word. Everything the book will teach, it teaches to someone who has already begun.
screen: `A SUTRA IS A THREAD.` · `WHO WAS PATANJALI? WE DON'T KNOW MUCH.` · `ATHA: NOW, THE TEACHING BEGINS.` · `YOGA ISN'T AFTER YOUR LIFE. IT'S THE SORTING.` · then, large: `ATHA YOGĀNUŚĀSANAM.`

segments.voice: Sit exactly as you are. Don't fix your posture first, don't wait for the room to be quiet. Now. Notice what's here: the sound nearest to you, the feeling in your hands, the mood you brought in. Whenever your mind leaves for later or for earlier, say the word to yourself, gently: now. And come back. That's all. You'll probably say it many times. Every time counts as starting. If you pray, you can offer this now to God. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1. Atha yoga anushasanam: now, the teaching of yoga. The first thread of the Yoga Sutras, and the first word is now.
Your line: now. Today, pick one thing you've been saving for a better time, and give it five minutes. Now. Day two hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: The Yoga Sutras are studied line by line with a teacher and a commentary, often chanted in Sanskrit first; many yoga schools, in India and around the world, open their study with the first sutra.

fork.setup: you've wanted to start a daily practice for a year. when does Patanjali's book say to begin?
fork.reveal: the first word of the Yoga Sutras is atha: now. the teaching starts with someone who has already begun.

original.note: Sanskrit: atha, now + yoga + anushasana, teaching or instruction. Yoga Sutra 1.1.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'now' is just a filler word to get the book going.
what it means: the teaching begins here, for someone who has already arrived, as they are.
what a scholar hears: atha is a traditional opening marker, also auspicious; the commentary ascribed to Vyasa reads it as signaling the start of a subject (adhikara).

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 1.1 with the Vyasa commentary (atha as the start of the subject)

notes: Dating of the Yoga Sutras: scholarly estimates range roughly from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE; the script says 'from about twenty-two hundred years ago to about fifteen hundred'. Confirm.
Number of sutras: 195 or 196 depending on the recension; the script says 'about a hundred and ninety-five'.
Tradition identifies Patanjali with Adishesha (Ananta), the serpent; confirm the phrasing 'the great serpent who holds up the world'.
The Sanskrit of 1.1 is quoted in the original (public domain); transliteration spelled for listening in the voice.
